item.what_it_does: Ensures an edgeJoin node sees its two parents in (base, join) order — once when ordering the raw edge list, and again when ordering a node's source_names/ids inside _node_to_code.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL double-work. `_order_edge_join_incoming_edges` already reorders each edgeJoin's incoming edges to [base, join] using resolve_edge_join_role_indices, and graph_to_code_multi runs it on every edge list (lines 925, 977, 999) BEFORE building node_sources/node_source_ids. Then `_node_to_code` (line 386) calls `_role_order_node_sources`, which calls resolve_edge_join_role_indices a SECOND time on the already-ordered sources to reorder them again. The second pass is a no-op whenever the first ran (sources are already base-first), but it re-does the full role resolution and re-raises on the same conditions.
item.current_metrics: _order_edge_join_incoming_edges len 33 cx ~9; _role_order_node_sources len 19 cx ~4; resolve_edge_join_role_indices invoked 2x per edgeJoin per save
item.proposal: Pick ONE ordering authority. Since `_order_edge_join_incoming_edges` already guarantees edge order at the graph-assembly layer for every path, drop the re-ordering in `_role_order_node_sources` and keep only a cheap assertion (len(names)==len(ids)) — or, conversely, delete the edge-level pass and rely solely on per-node ordering. Document which layer owns role order.
item.behavior_preservation: When _order_edge_join_incoming_edges has run (always, in graph_to_code/_multi), source_names are already [base, join], so _role_order_node_sources returns them unchanged — removing it yields identical output. Direct unit-test callers of _node_to_code that bypass the edge pass are the only behavioural delta; the edge-level pass can be made the single guarantee by having those tests route through it (or keep a one-line role-resolve only when an edgeJoin node is passed unordered). The role-resolution error conditions remain enforced once at the surviving site.
item.est_reduction: ~20 LOC; removes a redundant resolve_edge_join_role_indices call per edgeJoin

verdict.evidence:
The redundancy is REAL on production paths. graph_to_code (codegen.py:925) and graph_to_code_multi (977, 999) all run _order_edge_join_incoming_edges before building node_sources/ids; then _node_to_code:386 calls _role_order_node_sources, which calls resolve_edge_join_role_indices a 2nd time. resolve_edge_join_role_indices (_edge_join.py:61-98) returns indices purely from config: source_ids.index(baseInput), source_ids.index(joinInput). The target_handles arg (passed only at the edge level, line 642-646) just triggers validate_edge_join_target_handles VALIDATION — it does NOT change the returned ordering. So after the edge pass orders edges base-first, _build_node_sources/_build_node_source_ids yield base-first lists, and the node pass re-resolves to [0,1] = no-op. Proposal's "incidental double-work" diagnosis is correct for the happy path.

BUT the proposal's RECOMMENDED form — "drop the re-ordering in _role_order_node_sources and keep only a cheap assertion len(names)==len(ids)" — is NOT behavior-preserving:
(1) _role_order_node_sources is not just a reorder; via resolve_edge_join_role_indices it ENFORCES correctness invariants (exactly-2 inputs, distinct inputs, baseInput/joinInput present+connected) and raises an enriched ParseError carrying source_names/source_ids (codegen.py:435-442). A bare length assertion removes this.
(2) The edge layer does NOT enforce those invariants on every path: _order_edge_join_incoming_edges line 636 `if len(group) != 2: ordered.extend(group); continue` SKIPS resolve_edge_join_role_indices entirely for 1-input/3-input edgeJoins. For that case the node-level resolution is currently the catcher. After reducing to a length check, a 1/3-input edgeJoin would flow to _gen_edge_join (_codegen_builders.py:1050) which still raises on len(source_names)!=2, so it stays loud — but with a DIFFERENT, less specific error and lost role/id context. That is an observable behavior change, not a pure internal refactor.
(3) Cross-boundary submodel inputs are appended to sm_node_sources/sm_node_source_ids AFTER the edge ordering (codegen.py:1013-1043), so the node layer is the only place those late-added edgeJoin sources get role-resolved.
(4) The builder's own comments (_codegen_builders.py:1062, 1074-1078) explicitly state "_role_order_node_sources has already resolved baseInput/joinInput ... and ordered sources base-first, so source_names[0]/[1] ARE the base and join nodes". _gen_edge_join then does `base_name, join_name = source_names` — so the ordering is correctness-critical (a base/join swap = silently wrong join), not cosmetic. Degrading the surviving site to a length check makes those comments false.

Test coverage of the delta: ALL edgeJoin codegen tests route through graph_to_code/graph_to_code_multi (test_edge_join.py:226,325,364,395,426,513,528,764) — i.e. through the edge pass. There are NO direct _node_to_code/_gen_edge_join callers in the suite that pass mis-ordered edgeJoin sources. So removing _role_order_node_sources would break NO existing test — which is exactly the silent-regression risk CLAUDE.md ("fail loudly, no fallbacks") warns against: the node-level resolution is the single guarantee protecting any non-graph caller of the _node_to_code seam (used by _submodel_node_to_code:879). The "fail loudly" tests at :368/:399 use the 2-input branch (edges without handles), so the edge pass — not the node pass — is what raises there today; that supports the 2-input redundancy claim but says nothing about the !=2 / cross-boundary paths.
verdict.est_reduction: ~15-20 LOC and one redundant resolve_edge_join_role_indices call per edgeJoin per save — ONLY achievable safely by consolidating to a single full-resolution authority, NOT by the proposed reduce-to-length-assertion (which would be ~20 LOC but changes error/enforcement behavior).
verdict.repro_path: Construct an edgeJoin GraphNode with config baseInput/joinInput, then call _node_to_code(node, source_names=[join_name, base_name], source_ids=[join_id, base_id]) directly (reversed order, bypassing _order_edge_join_incoming_edges). Today _role_order_node_sources reorders to base-first so _gen_edge_join emits base_input=base_name correctly. With the node pass reduced to a length assertion, the reversed order would survive and _gen_edge_join would bind base_name,join_name = reversed sources, emitting a base/join-swapped join. No existing test exercises this path, so the regression is silent.
verdict.recommended_action: Do NOT apply the recommended "reduce to length assertion" form — it drops enforced role resolution and enriched error context at the node layer for the !=2-input and cross-boundary-submodel paths (silent base/join swap risk). If pursuing the cleanup, pick the SINGLE-AUTHORITY consolidation: either keep _role_order_node_sources doing full resolve_edge_join_role_indices and DELETE the edge-level pass (after auditing that _topo_sort/connect_pairs/node_source_ids tolerate unordered edges and adding a direct-call regression test), or keep the edge pass and have _node_to_code's edgeJoin branch trust it — but in EITHER case first add a failing test at the direct-call boundary (reversed-order _node_to_code edgeJoin -> base/join swap) per CLAUDE.md TDD, since the current suite would not catch the regression. Document which layer owns role order.

verdict.evidence:
Re-read src/haute/codegen.py:122-176 in full and traced every case.

INCIDENTAL vs ESSENTIAL: The complexity IS genuinely incidental. The function must distinguish four essential cases (parent_name_by_id is None -> verbatim pass-through; parent_id is a known id -> remap to name; parent_id already equals a current name -> keep; else -> stale), but the 4-5 levels of nesting and the duplicated set-computation are removable. Extracting the loop (139-149) into _remap_inputs_by_parent and the post-loop reconciliation (150-171) into _resolve_stale_ownership is a standard flatten.

BEHAVIOR-PRESERVATION (proven, every branch):
1. Line 128 opaque guard, line 135 `inputs_by_parent is not None` guard, and the final `if inputs_by_parent:` write are all outside the extracted helpers and unchanged.
2. The two set computations the proposal targets ARE value-identical: line 136 uses `parent_name_by_id is not None`, line 151 uses truthiness `parent_name_by_id`. They diverge ONLY when parent_name_by_id == {} (empty dict): line136 -> set({}.values()) == set(); line151 -> set() (bool({}) is False). Both yield set(). For None both yield set(). For non-empty both yield set(values). So `parent_names` == `current_parent_names` ALWAYS; computing once is value-identical. The line-169 warning payload `connected_parent_names=sorted(parent_names)` is unaffected.
3. Loop semantics (id->name remap, `elif parent_id in parent_names` keep-as-name, else append-stale-and-continue) are preserved verbatim in the helper.

item.what_it_does: Submodel-context code is generated as @pipeline.* then string-replaced to @submodel.* (and, for instances inside submodels, @pipeline.->@<obj>.).
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL. Codegen emits everything with a hardcoded `@pipeline.`/`pipeline.` prefix and then does targeted `.replace('@pipeline.', '@submodel.', 1)` / `.replace('pipeline._apply_edge_join(', 'submodel._apply_edge_join(')` fixups in 3 places. item.current_metrics: 3 separate replace sites; _submodel_node_to_code exists only to do 2 replaces
item.proposal: Thread the decorator object name (`pipeline`/`submodel`) into the per-node builders (or pass it to `_generate_node_code`) so bodies are emitted with the correct prefix directly, eliminating `_submodel_node_to_code`'s two replaces and the inline instance replace at 757. The `_apply_edge_join` receiver then also comes out correct without a second replace.
item.behavior_preservation: Emitting `@submodel.` directly yields the same text as emitting `@pipeline.` then replacing the first occurrence — provided the decorator is always first, which it is (the contract kwarg is injected into that same decorator). Edge-join body uses `pipeline._apply_edge_join`; parameterising the receiver produces `submodel._apply_edge_join` identically. Round-trip property tests guard equivalence.

verdict.evidence: The proposal's premise is factually wrong about WHERE the `@pipeline.`/`pipeline.` prefix originates. It is NOT controlled by `_generate_node_code` (codegen.py:468, which merely dispatches `entry.codegen(node, source_names)`) nor by `_node_to_code`. It is hardcoded as string literals in ~27 sites across ~22 registered codegen builders in src/haute/_codegen_builders.py: e.g. f"@pipeline.model_score(...)" (650), f"@pipeline.rating_step(...)" (764), f"@pipeline.scenario_expander(...)" (837), f"@pipeline.output(...)" (983), the EDGE_JOIN body f"    return pipeline._apply_edge_join(...)" (1090), plus ~13 module-level template constants (_LIVE_SWITCH, _MODEL_SCORE, _BANDING_*, _RATING_STEP, _SINK_*, _OPTIMISER*, _CONSTANT, _EXTERNAL_FILE...). The builder contract is `CodegenBuilder = Callable[[GraphNode, list[str]], str]` (_codegen_builders.py:476). To "thread obj_name into the per-node builders" one must widen this registry-dispatched callable signature AND edit every builder + every template constant (~40 sites) to interpolate f"@{obj_name}." — to delete 3 `.replace()` calls and a 15-line wrapper. The escape hatch "(or pass it to _generate_node_code)" is impossible: _generate_node_code receives an already-baked opaque string from the builder and cannot inject a prefix without... string replacement, which is what already exists. So the "~15 LOC removed" claim is net FALSE — it is a large LOC INCREASE plus a contract-type change. Separately, the existing replace design IS behaviour-preserving and well-guarded: the decorator is always line 1 (contract kwarg is injected into that same first @pipeline./@submodel. line by _inject_contract_kwarg, codegen.py:258-260), so `.replace("@pipeline.","@submodel.",1)` (880) and the instance replace at 757 (`@pipeline.instance(` is line 1) map 1:1; the edge-join `.replace("pipeline._apply_edge_join(",...)` (882) has exactly one occurrence per body. Regression guards exist: test_edge_join.py:516 asserts `"pipeline._apply_edge_join" not in files["modules/rating.py"]` and :517 asserts the submodel form IS present; round-trip property tests reload submodel files where the symbol `pipeline` is undefined, catching any stray leak. Net: the 3 replaces are a deliberate LOCALIZED ADAPTER that keeps ~22 builders prefix-agnostic via a single chokepoint; collapsing it smears prefix-handling across ~40 builder/template sites — readability and risk get WORSE, not better. A legitimate (but different and much smaller) cleanup would be to fold the 3 replaces into one shared helper `_rewrite_pipeline_prefix(code, obj_name)` reused by _submodel_node_to_code and the instance path; that is worth maybe 3-5 LOC and zero builder churn. The proposal AS WRITTEN (thread name into builders / _generate_node_code) is unsound in mechanism and false in its LOC/effort claims; only the weaker centralize-the-replaces variant has value, hence marginal not unsound.

item.title: Main-file root-node source_ids carry the UNRESOLVED submodel placeholder id while source_names carry the resolved child func name, so _parent_name_by_id builds a wrong id->name map and the emitted contract drops/mis-attributes inputs_by_parent ownership
item.location: src/haute/codegen.py:1181-1183 (root_node_sources appends resolved `src_name` from actual_src, but root_node_source_ids appends raw `edge.source`); consumed by codegen.py:408-411 (_node_to_code -> _parent_name_by_id(source_ids, source_names)) and 122-176 (_format_contract_source stale-parent reconciliation)
item.failure_scenario: A root node is fed across a submodel boundary (edge.source = 'submodel__M', sourceHandle='out__child7'). The single-file and submodel-internal paths build node_sources and node_source_ids from the SAME e.source so they align, but on the main-file path root_node_sources gets the resolved child func name (line 1182) while root_node_source_ids gets 'submodel__M' (line 1183). _parent_name_by_id zips them into {'submodel__M': 'child7_func'}. item.title: _inject_contract_kwarg targets the first line whose lstrip starts with '@pipeline.'/'@submodel.', so user code containing such a line (in a string/comment/decorated inner def) hijacks contract injection into the user body instead of the node decorator
item.location: src/haute/codegen.py:258-301 (_inject_contract_kwarg line scan); reached from codegen.py:412-414 (_node_to_code) for builders that embed user code, e.g. _codegen_builders.py:648-661 (_gen_model_score user-code branch), 761-772 (_gen_rating_step), 836-842 (_gen_scenario_expander), 1031-1038 (_gen_transform)
item.failure_scenario: A POLARS/modelScore/ratingStep/scenarioExpander node's user code contains a line that lstrips to '@pipeline.' — e.g. a comment `# @pipeline.polars does X`, or a triple-quoted/docstring/string literal line `text = """@pipeline.foo"""`, or a nested decorated helper `@pipeline.something` the user pasted. _inject_contract_kwarg iterates lines and injects the contract kwarg into the FIRST such line, which is now inside the function body rather than the real node decorator. If that line has no '(' it appends `(contract=...)` to a comment/string line; if it has '(' it splices the kwarg into the user's parenthesised expression. Result is either a SyntaxError (caught by the emit gate -> save fails loudly with a confusing 'codegen bug' message for valid user code) or, worse, syntactically-valid-but-wrong code where the node decorator never receives its contract kwarg and a user expression is mutated. The real node decorator is always physically first in the emitted block, so the scan should anchor to the decorator preceding `def {func_name}` rather than the first textual match.

item.title: _gen_live_switch picks the active param via the FIRST input_scenario_map entry whose scenario=='live', but the executor (_build_live_switch) iterates the map for scenario==ctx.source; when two inputs are both mapped 'live' the codegen and executor can select different frames even under a normal live run
item.location: src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:529-539 (_gen_live_switch: `for inp, scn in input_scenario_map.items(): if scn=='live' and inp in source_names: active_param=inp; break`) vs src/haute/_builders.py:649-664 (_build_live_switch loops `for inp, scn in input_scenario_map.items(): if scn==_source:` then inner-loops source order)
item.failure_scenario: Catalog #1 covers the batch-vs-live divergence (standalone always routes 'live'). This is a DISTINCT case under the SAME source='live': the generated body breaks on the first map entry mapped 'live' that is in source_names, keyed by dict insertion order of input_scenario_map. The executor instead, for each (inp,scn) with scn=='live', scans input_names (edge/source order) for a name==inp and returns dfs at that index. If input_scenario_map maps two distinct inputs to 'live' (a misconfiguration the code does not reject), or if map insertion order differs from source_names order, codegen's first-map-entry winner and the executor's first-map-entry-resolved-against-source-order winner can be different frames — a silent mispricing in the live path itself, not just batch. Neither side validates uniqueness of the 'live' assignment, so the equivalence depends on an unstated single-live-input invariant.

verdict.evidence: Drove the REAL _gen_live_switch (src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:529-532) and _build_live_switch.switch_fn (src/haute/_builders.py:649-653) over 15 adversarial source='live' combinations. Every case agreed. Key repro outputs: two-live A-first map={'a':'live','b':'live'} src=['a','b'] => codegen->'a' executor->'a'; two-live B-first map={'b':'live','a':'live'} src=['a','b'] => codegen->'b' executor->'b'; SAME two maps with src reversed to ['b','a'] => still codegen->'a'/'a' and 'b'/'b' (source order does NOT change the winner); ghost-live-first map={'ghost':'live','real':'live'} src=['real'] => codegen->'real' executor->'real'; three-input interleaved {'x':'live','y':'batch','z':'live'} both src orders => codegen->'x' executor->'x'; fallback no-live-entry {'a':'batch','b':'batch'} src=['a','b'] => 'a'/'a' (executor logs live_switch_unmapped_scenario falling_back_to=a, == codegen first_param). ZERO divergences. Root cause: both functions iterate input_scenario_map.items() in identical INSERTION order and select the FIRST 'live' entry whose input is in source_names — codegen via the explicit `inp in source_names` guard, the executor implicitly (its inner input_names loop fails to resolve ghost entries and falls through to the next map entry). The executor's inner loop over input_names only resolves the chosen entry's positional INDEX; it never alters WHICH entry wins, so the claim's 'resolved against source order' divergence mechanism does not exist. The two-live misconfig is genuinely unvalidated (deploy/_pruner.py:42-44 takes first only; no uniqueness check anywhere) but both sides deterministically pick the same first 'live' entry. Catalog #1 (codegen always-live vs executor source-routed) is the real, distinct bug, keyed on source!='live'; B3's same-source='live' divergence claim is false.

item.title: _rewrite_single_return_source matches passthrough return lines by the literal prefix '    return ' AND `not startswith('    return pl.')`, so an optimiserApply whose passthrough source variable is named `pl` (or any future `return pl<x>`) is mis-counted, raising a spurious 'expected exactly one passthrough return line' codegen error
item.location: src/haute/codegen.py:348-365 (_rewrite_single_return_source); invoked from codegen.py:389-395 (_node_to_code when _optimiser_apply_ratebook_return_source resolves a name)
item.failure_scenario: The passthrough optimiserApply template emits `    return {first}` where {first} is the sanitized func-name of the ratebook input node. The rewrite locates the single return line by `line.startswith('    return ') and not line.startswith('    return pl.')` — the `pl.` exclusion exists to skip Polars-expression returns. But _sanitize_func_name can legitimately produce a source name beginning with `pl` (e.g. a node labelled 'PL Rates' -> `pl_rates`, giving `    return pl_rates`). `'    return pl_rates'.startswith('    return pl.')` is False, so that line IS counted — fine here — but a node sanitizing to exactly `pl` would yield `    return pl` which does not start with `    return pl.` so is counted (ok), whereas a node yielding `    return pl.` is impossible. The real fragility: the heuristic conflates 'this is a passthrough return of a variable' with 'string does not start with return pl.', which is a brittle proxy. A template change that emits any helper line like `    return pl.LazyFrame()` for an unconfigured branch, OR a body with two passthrough-shaped returns, makes the `len(return_lines)!=1` guard raise HauteError on otherwise-valid configs. testable by feeding a graph whose ratebook-input node label sanitizes such that the body contains an unexpected count of `    return ` lines.

verdict.repro_path: C:\Users\prici\haute\review\03-simplification\repro\codegen__B4.py
verdict.evidence: Executed repro (exit 0, claim CONFIRMED). _rewrite_single_return_source (src/haute/codegen.py:348-365) finds the passthrough line via `line.startswith("    return ") and not line.startswith("    return pl.")`. The optimiserApply docstring is built from the user-controlled NodeData.description through _sanitize_description (src/haute/_codegen_builders.py:131-182), which preserves embedded newlines VERBATIM (it only doubles backslashes, escapes double-quotes, and conditionally prepends "\n" -- NO neutralisation of `return` lines). CONTROL run (plain description) -> codegen OK, rewrite correctly emits `    return ratebook_src`. TRIGGER run -- identical graph, ONLY the description changed to `"summary line\n    return me_from_docstring"` -- emits a docstring whose 2nd physical line is `    return me_from_docstring` (4-space indent, not `pl.`), which the heuristic counts. Repro output: "HauteError: optimiserApply codegen expected exactly one passthrough return line. (return_line_count=2)". So _node_to_code raises a SPURIOUS codegen error for an otherwise-valid optimiserApply graph. To exercise the rewrite I set optimiser_mode="ratebook" (bypasses the sourceType in {run,registered} & !=ratebook early-return at codegen.py:319-324) with ratebook_input="rb_node" matching a connected source id. No upstream guard prevents this: the description sanitizer is purpose-built for multi-line fidelity and intentionally keeps newlines. NOTE: the claim's own concrete examples (`pl_rates`, `pl`, func-name/{first} path) are all SAFE -- the real reachable trigger is the description field, which the claim under-emphasises (it framed the live risk as a hypothetical future template change). The defect (brittle proxy mis-counting `    return ` lines) is nonetheless real and reachable today.
verdict.est_reduction: n/a (bug verification, not a simplification)
verdict.recommended_action: Confirm as a NEW low-severity robustness bug (distinct from catalog #2/#3, which describe the opposite failure: the passthrough body being a silent runtime no-op; no catalog entry covers this spurious-error miscount). Fix: stop using a string-prefix proxy to locate the passthrough return. Either (a) operate on the function BODY only -- e.g. parse with ast / locate the single top-level `return` statement of the generated def rather than scanning all physical lines, so docstring/description content can never be miscounted; or (b) since codegen knows the exact passthrough source name it just emitted, target the literal line `    return {first}` (or rewrite by AST node) instead of any `    return ` line. Per repo TDD policy, first add a failing test: an optimiserApply node whose description contains an indented `return ...` line (e.g. a pasted code snippet) must still codegen and must rewrite the real passthrough to the ratebook input. This also future-proofs against the template-change fragility the claim raises.

item.what_it_does: Validates the v2 schema before shredding/writing.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL: validate_v2_schema runs three times on the same config in one build. build_per_port_cache validates at line 776, then the no-op trapdoor's is_per_port_cache_valid path does not validate but the live build path calls shred_to_buffers (line 826) which validates AGAIN at line 561. validate is O(tables*columns) with regex path parsing — pure waste on the hot rebuild path, and it muddies which layer owns the invariant.
item.current_metrics: validate_v2_schema cx22, len 140; called 2-3x per build.
item.proposal: Make the public entry points (build_per_port_cache, load_v2_api_source) the single validation boundary and give shred_to_buffers a private already-validated variant, OR keep shred_to_buffers self-validating (it is also called from tests directly) but drop the redundant validate at build_per_port_cache:776 since the very next thing build does is call shred_to_buffers which validates. Document the single owner in the docstring.
item.behavior_preservation: validate_v2_schema is a pure, idempotent guard that either raises ApiInputSchemaError or returns None; running it once vs twice on the same dict produces identical control flow and identical exceptions. The earliest-raising call already fires before any disk write, so removing the later duplicate cannot let a malformed config reach the writer.
item.est_reduction: 1 call removed; ~0 LOC but removes O(n) redundant work and a confusing 'who validates' question.

verdict.evidence:
Re-read in full: validate_v2_schema (_api_input_schema.py:263-403, file ends at 403) is a pure idempotent guard — only raises ApiInputSchemaError or returns None, no mutation/IO/global state; running it N times on one dict is identical. So the LIVE build path is genuinely redundant: build_per_port_cache validates at :776, then shred_to_buffers validates AGAIN at :561 (reached via :826). That part of the premise is correct.

BUT the proposal misidentifies the redundant call and its main option breaks behavior:

(1) Line 776 is NOT redundant with the route. The /build route (routes/json_cache.py:344-388) does NOT call validate_v2_schema; _select_v2_config (:236) only READS the config. The route's documented error case 3 ("schema validation -> 422", :353) is satisfied solely by build_per_port_cache catching ApiInputSchemaError. So :776 IS the public/route validation boundary; the true duplicate is the internal call at shred_to_buffers:561.

(2) Proposal Option 2 ("drop the redundant validate at build_per_port_cache:776") is NOT behavior-preserving. is_per_port_cache_valid (:1034-1077) does NOT validate (confirmed: it only checks _v2_fingerprint + _data_file_matches + table_is_emitting). item.what_it_does: Builds the build-summary payload ({schema_mode, schema_fingerprint, tables, data_file, skipped}) and the meta.json payload.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL triplication of one dict shape. The no-op-trapdoor return (793-800) reconstructs the summary from existing_meta with per-key .get defaults; meta_payload (865-871) builds it from fresh values; the success return (895-902) repeats the same five keys plus cache_dir. Three literal copies of the same contract drift the moment a sixth field is added.
item.current_metrics: 3 near-identical ~7-line dict literals (~21 LOC); build_per_port_cache len 155.
item.proposal: Introduce one builder `_build_summary(*, schema_mode, fingerprint, tables, data_file, skipped, cache_dir) -> dict` and a `_summary_from_meta(meta, cache_dir)` adapter for the no-op path. meta_payload becomes `_build_summary(...)` minus cache_dir (or include and pop), and both returns call the same builder.
item.behavior_preservation: Output dicts are assembled from the same values in the same key order; meta.json currently omits cache_dir and the returns include it, so the builder must parametrise that one key. The no-op path's `.get(...)` defaults ({} / 'v2' / '') are preserved verbatim in `_summary_from_meta`. JSON serialisation of meta.json is key-order-independent for readers, so factoring does not change on-disk bytes' meaning.
item.est_reduction: ~12 LOC; single source of the summary contract.

verdict.evidence:
Re-read all three sites in src/haute/_json_shred.py: no-op return (793-800), meta_payload (865-871), success return (895-902). The 5-key contract (schema_mode, schema_fingerprint, tables, data_file, skipped) is triplicated; this is INCIDENTAL — there is no semantic reason for three literal copies. The only real differences are parametrisable: (a) value source (existing_meta vs fresh in-memory) and (b) the cache_dir key (present in both returns, absent in meta_payload).

The proposal is behavior-preserving AS SPECIFIED because it correctly introduces TWO helpers, not one: a fresh-value _build_summary(...) for meta_payload and the success return, and a separate _summary_from_meta(meta, cache_dir) adapter for the no-op path. This is essential: the no-op path's values come from existing_meta.get(...) with defaults, NOT from the fresh parameters — a single shared builder could not serve it. Traced each case:
- No-op (793-800): the .get defaults must be preserved verbatim — schema_mode→"v2", schema_fingerprint→"", tables→[], data_file→ bare .get (None default), skipped→{"records":0,"rows_by_table":{}}. The proposal explicitly says "preserved verbatim in _summary_from_meta". Correct. (read_per_port_cache_meta at 1235 can return a dict missing keys / partially-populated, so these defaults are load-bearing for a corrupt/pre-W2 meta.)
- meta_payload (865-871): fresh values, NO cache_dir, consumed only by orjson.dumps into meta.json (872). An extra cache_dir key would change on-disk bytes, so it must be excluded/popped — the proposal acknowledges this ("minus cache_dir (or include and pop)"). Correct.
- Success return (895-902): identical fresh values + cache_dir. schema_mode is hardcoded "v2" in the fresh path, consistent with the no-op default.

No consumer depends on dict identity or key ordering: the sole summary consumer (routes/json_cache.py:268-296) reads strictly by key (summary["skipped"], summary.get("tables"), t.get("row_count")); meta.json readers is_per_port_cache_valid (1062-1066) and read_per_port_cache_meta (1246-1251) also use .get, so key order is irrelevant to behavior. To keep meta.json BYTES byte-identical, _build_summary should emit keys in the same order (schema_mode, schema_fingerprint, tables, data_file, skipped[, cache_dir]); even a reordering would be behaviorally safe for all readers, but order-preservation is the zero-diff choice. No site has side effects or except-path coupling to the dict literal (the BaseException cleanup at 873-875 is orthogonal). skip_stats.as_meta() (215-220) yields exactly {"records":..,"rows_by_table":..}, matching the no-op default shape.

Conclusion: incidental triplication, provably behavior-preserving given the proposal's three named constraints (verbatim .get defaults, cache_dir parametrised/popped, key order for byte-identity), and worthwhile (single source of a contract that the docstring itself warns will drift when a 6th field is added).
verdict.est_reduction: ~12 LOC net (replaces ~21 LOC of dict literals with one ~7-line builder + a small adapter); collapses 3 copies of the 5-key contract to 1 source.
verdict.recommended_action: Proceed. Implement exactly as specified with both helpers: _build_summary(*, schema_mode, fingerprint, tables, data_file, skipped, cache_dir=None) returning the 5 keys in their current order plus cache_dir only when provided (or build full + pop for meta_payload); and _summary_from_meta(meta, cache_dir) that preserves all five .get defaults VERBATIM (note the bare data_file .get with None default and the non-empty skipped default). Keep meta_payload's serialised key order so meta.json bytes are unchanged. Guard against regression: a TDD failing test should (1) assert all three outputs key-for-key on a fresh build AND a no-op rebuild, and (2) assert meta.json bytes are byte-identical before/after the refactor for a representative build, and (3) cover a partial/corrupt existing_meta so the .get defaults are exercised.

item.what_it_does: For each value at a table's iteration depth, emits a row to every table at that depth, distinguishing scalar-value tables from object tables.

item.current_metrics: _walk len 39, cx15, nest 7 (top-10 nesting hotspot).
item.proposal: Compute is_scalar_table once when building tables_by_path: store `(label, col_specs, is_scalar_table)` (or a tiny frozen dataclass) in tables_by_path[path]. _walk then reads the precomputed flag, flattening the two `any(...)` scans into a field access and making the scalar-vs-object branch self-documenting.
item.behavior_preservation: is_scalar_table is fully determined by col_specs at construction time and col_specs never changes during the walk, so precomputing yields the identical boolean at every use. item.est_reduction: ~4 LOC and removes O(records*cols) repeated scanning; modest cx/nest reduction in the hottest inner loop.

item.what_it_does: Streams one JSON value out of a root array, tracking brace/bracket depth and returning the terminating delimiter.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL dead branch. At depth 0 a `]` byte is already handled by the `if b in {b'}', b']'}` block (lines 472-479): depth is not > 0, so it falls to `if b == b']': return ...` at 477-478. The later guard `if depth == 0 and b in {b',', b']'}` (line 481) can therefore NEVER see `]` — only `,` reaches it. The `b']'` member is unreachable, which misleads a reader into thinking close-bracket termination happens in two places.
item.current_metrics: function len ~49, cx ~12; one redundant set membership on a hot per-byte loop.
item.proposal: Change line 481 to `if depth == 0 and b == b',':` (drop the unreachable `b']'`). Optionally add a one-line comment that `]` at depth 0 is handled above.
item.behavior_preservation: Provably equivalent: the only byte that can reach line 481 with depth==0 is one not in {'"','{','[','}',']'}; for `]` the earlier block returns first, so removing `]` from the set cannot change any reachable outcome. The `,` path and the returned (buf, delimiter) tuple are unchanged.
item.est_reduction: 0 net LOC; removes a genuinely unreachable condition that costs reader-confusion and a redundant comparison.

verdict.evidence:
Re-read src/haute/_json_shred.py:436-484 (the whole function) and the sole caller at 380-433. The author's reachability claim is correct and the `b']'` member at line 481 is provably dead.

Control flow for any non-in-string byte b: line 462 intercepts `"`; line 467 intercepts `{`/`[`; line 472 `if b in {b"}", b"]"}` intercepts EVERY `}`/`]` byte unconditionally (the test is purely on b's value, independent of depth). That 472-479 block is exhaustive for `]`: if depth>0 it decrements+continues (476); if depth==0 it returns at 478 (`if b == b']': return ...`). There is NO path where a `]` byte falls through to line 481. (In-string `]`/`}` are appended+continued at 452-460, so they never reach 467/472/481 either.)

Therefore line 481 is only ever evaluated for bytes that are not `"`,`{`,`[`,`}`,`]`. For those bytes `b in {b",", b"]"}` is identically equal to `b == b','` because `b == b']'` is impossible there. Replacing line 481 with `if depth == 0 and b == b',':` yields the same truth value for every reachable byte, the same return tuple `(bytes(buf).rstrip(), b)`, and the same fall-through to `buf.extend(b)` at 484. Behavior is preserved on all inputs.

Traced the non-obvious cases to be sure: (a) `]` terminating a bare scalar element, e.g. `[1]` -> first=`1`, depth=0, the `]` is caught at 472 and returned at 478 with delimiter `]` (NOT via 481), exactly as today. (b) `,` after a scalar, e.g. `[1,2]` -> reaches 481, depth==0, returns `(b"1", b",")` — unchanged. (c) `,` at depth>0 (inside a nested object/array) -> reaches 481, depth!=0, falls to 484 and is appended — unchanged; the `depth == 0` guard is essential and is correctly retained. (d) `}` at depth==0 still raises at 479; (e) strings/escapes handled at 452-460 untouched.

The `depth == 0` guard MUST stay (the proposal keeps it). The only thing removed is the unreachable `b']'` set member plus one redundant per-byte set-membership comparison on the hot loop. No test references this function (none in tests/), so no test churn; the equivalence is a pure code-trace result.
verdict.est_reduction: 0 net LOC (replaces a 2-element set/membership with a single `==` comparison on the hot per-byte loop; removes one provably-unreachable condition). +1 LOC if the optional clarifying comment is added. Clarity/correctness-signal improvement, not a size win.

verdict.recommended_action: Apply: change line 481 to `if depth == 0 and b == b",":` and add a one-line comment noting that a depth-0 `]` is handled by the close-delimiter block above (lines 472-479). Keep the `depth == 0` guard. Optionally add a regression test exercising `[1]`, `[1,2]`, and a nested-object array to lock in delimiter semantics, since the function is currently untested.

The filename math `cd / f"{_sanitise_label(label)}.parquet"` is indeed identical at all three sites, so the `_parquet_path_for_label` part is genuinely incidental and sound: build's label is a guaranteed str (validate_v2_schema is called first at 776/561 and rejects non-str labels), and load/validity each apply their own isinstance(label,str) guard BEFORE deriving the path, so a shared `_parquet_path_for_label(cd,label)` preserves behavior everywhere (~2 net LOC saved).

But the proposed `_iter_emitting_labels(v2_config) -> Iterator[str]` (which filters BOTH table_is_emitting AND isinstance(label,str)) BREAKS a test-locked behavioral divergence between the two loops. load_per_port_cache CONTINUES (skips) on a non-str label; is_per_port_cache_valid RETURNS FALSE on a non-str label. Two dedicated regression tests pin this exactly: tests/test_load_v2_api_source.py:165 test_load_per_port_cache_skips_non_string_label asserts frames=={} for label=123, and :141 test_is_per_port_cache_valid_rejects_non_string_label_on_emitting_table forces fingerprint+data-file to match so the label arm decides and asserts is_per_port_cache_valid(...) is False for label=123.

If both callers iterate a str-filtering _iter_emitting_labels, the non-str label is dropped by the helper, so is_per_port_cache_valid never sees a missing parquet and falls through to `return True` -> flips False->True, failing the :141 test (a silent validity pass on a config that must be rejected). The proposal's own caveat ("keep the validity caller's explicit `if not isinstance(label,str): return False`") is self-contradictory with its helper contract: once _iter_emitting_labels has filtered str, validity can never reach that explicit return-False. To preserve behavior the helper must NOT filter labels (yield raw table/label), but then it cannot be typed Iterator[str] and the str-guard cannot be shared, so the divergent skip-vs-return-False action stays per-caller and the loop-dedup largely evaporates. Hence the ~15 LOC headline depends on a unification that is unsound; only the ~2 LOC _parquet_path_for_label slice is safe, and even that needs re-specification rather than verbatim application.
verdict.est_reduction: Claimed ~15 LOC is not achievable safely. The behavior-preserving subset (_parquet_path_for_label only, applied at all three sites) saves ~2 net LOC. The _iter_emitting_labels loop-merge that drives the rest of the reduction is unsound.
verdict.repro_path: Apply the proposal as written (str-filtering _iter_emitting_labels shared by both loops), then run: pytest tests/test_load_v2_api_source.py::test_is_per_port_cache_valid_rejects_non_string_label_on_emitting_table -> FAILS (validity returns True instead of False). tests/test_load_v2_api_source.py::test_load_per_port_cache_skips_non_string_label still passes, demonstrating the asymmetry the helper cannot reconcile.
verdict.recommended_action: Reject the item as specified. Optionally re-scope to ONLY introduce `_parquet_path_for_label(cache_dir, label) -> Path` and call it at all three sites (build 845, load 962, validity 1074), leaving the two loops and their divergent non-str-label handling (load: continue; validity: return False) exactly as-is. Do NOT introduce a str-filtering _iter_emitting_labels shared across load and validity. If a label-iteration helper is still wanted, it must yield raw tables (not str-filtered) so each caller retains its own isinstance guard and divergent action; that yields little additional reduction. Keep the two existing regression tests as the guardrail.

item.what_it_does: Assembles the inferred tables[] list, choosing a scalar $value column for scalar-array depths and per-key columns for object depths.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL: the scalar-table branch (1200-1209) and the object-table branch (1211-1221) build a column dict literal with the SAME six keys ({name, path, type, status:'Inferred', selected:True, levels:None}) and differ only in name/path/type source; then both feed an identical tables.append({...}) with the same eight keys. The function is also a top-nesting hotspot (nest 7) because _walk's list/empty/object/scalar branching is inlined.
item.current_metrics: infer_v2_schema_from_data len 125, cx19, nest 7; inner _walk len 39, cx15, nest 7 (both top-15 nesting).
item.proposal: (a) Extract `_inferred_column(name, path, type) -> dict` so both branches call it, killing the duplicated six-key literal. (b) Extract `_columns_for_path(path_tuple, table_path, object_cols, scalar_tables) -> list[dict]` holding the scalar-vs-object decision, so the assembly loop body is two lines. (c) Optionally lift the empty/object/scalar-array classification in _walk into a small `_classify_array(items)` helper to flatten the elif ladder.
item.behavior_preservation: Both branches already emit status='Inferred', selected=True, levels=None; the helper hard-codes those identically. The scalar-vs-object selection (`path_tuple in scalar_tables and path_tuple not in object_cols`) is preserved verbatim. The nested-array ApiInputSchemaError is raised from the same point. Ordering of tables (sorted by (len(p), p)) and of columns (object_cols insertion order) is unchanged because the helper iterates the same dicts.
item.est_reduction: ~15-20 LOC; removes a 6-key duplicated literal and lowers nest depth of the assembly loop.

verdict.evidence:
Re-read src/haute/_json_shred.py:1108-1232 in full plus constants (72-73), the route consumer (routes/json_cache.py:534-540), and tests (test_scalar_array_and_inference.py).

verdict.est_reduction: ~15-20 LOC removed: eliminates the duplicated 6-key column literal and collapses the assembly-loop if/else (lowering the nest-7 hotspot to ~2 lines). Legit win on a top-15 hotspot (len 125, cx19).
verdict.recommended_action: Implement (a) _inferred_column(name, path, type)->dict and (b) _columns_for_path(...)->list[dict] as module-level (or nested) helpers. item.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:835-838 (build_per_port_cache legacy tmp cleanup) and :913-916 (_swap_dir_into_place legacy backup cleanup); functions build_per_port_cache / _swap_dir_into_place
item.what_it_does: Removes a stale fixed-name `<dir>.build-tmp` / `<dir>.build-old` left by an older non-unique-named build before staging a new one.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL: the 'compute legacy fixed-name sibling; if it exists rmtree it' pattern is written twice with the only difference being the suffix ('.build-tmp' vs '.build-old'). It is migration cruft from before the uuid-suffixed temp/backup names and reads as two unrelated blocks.
item.current_metrics: 2 x ~3-line blocks (~6 LOC).
item.proposal: Add `_clear_legacy_sibling(cache_dir: Path, suffix: str) -> None` that does `p = cache_dir.with_name(cache_dir.name + suffix); if p.exists(): shutil.rmtree(p)` and call it with '.build-tmp' and '.build-old'. (Even better: one `_clear_legacy_build_siblings(cache_dir)` clearing both, called once at build entry.)
item.behavior_preservation: Identical filesystem effect: same sibling names, same exists()-guarded rmtree, same call ordering relative to the unique-name staging. No new exception classes; rmtree raises exactly as before on a locked dir.
item.est_reduction: ~4 LOC; one named concept instead of two inline blocks.

verdict.evidence:
Re-read both cited blocks in full. Block A (src/haute/_json_shred.py:835-837, build_per_port_cache): `legacy_tmp_dir = cd.with_name(cd.name + ".build-tmp"); if legacy_tmp_dir.exists(): shutil.rmtree(legacy_tmp_dir)`. Block B (:913-915, _swap_dir_into_place): identical shape with `live_dir` and suffix ".build-old". The proposed `_clear_legacy_sibling(cache_dir, suffix)` = `p = cache_dir.with_name(cache_dir.name + suffix); if p.exists(): shutil.rmtree(p)`.

COMPLEXITY: genuinely INCIDENTAL — the two blocks are migration cruft from before the uuid-suffixed names (_unique_build_tmp_dir at :294-295 -> ".build-tmp-<uuid>"; _unique_build_old_dir at :298-299 -> ".build-old-<uuid>") and differ ONLY in the suffix string and the local var name (cd vs live_dir, both meaning "the cache dir"). Not essential.

BEHAVIOR-PRESERVING (two-call form): (1) path: with_name(name+suffix) byte-identical; (2) guard exists() identical (False on missing, follows symlinks) — same as inline; (3) shutil.rmtree with NO ignore_errors -> raises the exact same exception on a locked/permission-denied dir, propagating identically (the proposal's "rmtree raises exactly as before" holds because neither inline form passes ignore_errors); (4) ordering: block A stays strictly before tmp_dir=_unique_build_tmp_dir(cd) at :838; block B stays the first statement of _swap_dir_into_place before any rename — a function call at the same site preserves order, no early return, no swallowed exception; (5) no collision between fixed-name legacy paths and unique "-<uuid>" paths. Confirmed by tests test_leftover_build_tmp_from_crashed_build_is_cleaned (tests/test_json_cache_integrity.py:647) and test_leftover_build_old_backup_is_cleaned_on_next_swap (:664) which drive both blocks via public build_per_port_cache and assert the sibling is gone; the unique-name failure-injection swap tests (:682, :712) are untouched. So the two-call form passes the suite unchanged.

CAVEATS lowering it from sound to marginal: (a) est_reduction is overstated — helper adds ~4 LOC (def+body), removes two 3-LOC blocks and adds two 1-LOC calls => net ~1-2 LOC, not ~4; the win is "one named concept", not size. (b) The proposal's explicitly-suggested "even better: single _clear_legacy_build_siblings(cache_dir) clearing both, called once at build entry" is UNSOUND and must be rejected: block B's .build-old cleanup lives inside _swap_dir_into_place, which is a separate publish primitive invoked independently (imported and called directly in tests at :687/:717); folding it to build-entry would stop clearing .build-old when _swap_dir_into_place is called on its own AND move the cleanup earlier in the sequence — a behavior change. (c) Reviewers already flagged these fixed-name legacy paths as a concurrency concern (review/00-map/region-maps.json:880, leads/cache.json:136), so deleting the legacy blocks outright is a plausible better end-state than extracting them.
verdict.est_reduction: ~1-2 LOC net (proposal claims ~4; optimistic). True value is naming one concept, not size.
verdict.repro_path: tests/test_json_cache_integrity.py::test_leftover_build_tmp_from_crashed_build_is_cleaned and ::test_leftover_build_old_backup_is_cleaned_on_next_swap exercise both blocks via build_per_port_cache; both pass unchanged under the two-call helper form.
verdict.recommended_action: Adopt ONLY the two-call form: add `_clear_legacy_sibling(cache_dir: Path, suffix: str) -> None` and call it as `_clear_legacy_sibling(cd, ".build-tmp")` at :835 and `_clear_legacy_sibling(live_dir, ".build-old")` at :913 — provably behavior-preserving. REJECT the suggested single `_clear_legacy_build_siblings(...)` called once at build entry: it drops the independent .build-old cleanup when _swap_dir_into_place is invoked standalone and reorders it (a real behavior change). Given the small payoff and the standing concurrency flag on these fixed-name legacy paths, deferring in favor of eventually deleting the legacy blocks entirely is an equally reasonable choice.

item.what_it_does: Before strict-building each Polars Series, rejects values Polars would SILENTLY mis-coerce (bool into int/float; raw int into Date).
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL: the two guards are structurally identical — `if col_type in <set> and any(isinstance(v, <pytype>) for v in values): raise ApiInputSchemaError(<message>, column=..., declared_type=...)` — but written as two ~10-line blocks with prose-heavy messages inline, inflating the per-column loop body and burying the actual `pl.Series(...)` build.
item.current_metrics: _buffer_to_frame len ~58, cx high for its size; two ~10-line guard blocks.
item.proposal: Table-drive the silent-coercion guards: a module-level tuple `_SILENT_COERCION_GUARDS = ((frozenset({'int','float'}), bool, <msg_a>), (frozenset({'date'}), int, <msg_b>))` and a small loop `for types, pytype, msg in _SILENT_COERCION_GUARDS: if col_type in types and any(isinstance(v, pytype) for v in values): raise ApiInputSchemaError(msg.format(col=col_name, t=col_type), column=col_name, declared_type=col_type)`. The long messages move to named constants beside the table.
item.behavior_preservation: Same predicates, same exception type/kwargs, same messages. Order matters only between the bool guard and the date guard, and they are mutually exclusive on col_type (int/float vs date), so iteration order over the table cannot change which raises. bool-is-subclass-of-int nuance is preserved because the int guard checks `col_type in {int,float}` (not date) exactly as today; the date guard's `isinstance(v, int)` still catches bools-as-ints identically.
item.est_reduction: ~10 LOC out of the inner loop; the build statement becomes the visual focus.

verdict.est_reduction: ~10 LOC removed from the per-column loop body (two ~10-line guard blocks -> one ~4-line loop). NET module LOC roughly flat: the two long messages relocate to module-level string constants beside the table, so the win is loop-body LOCALITY (the pl.Series build becomes the visual focus), not total size.
verdict.evidence: Re-read src/haute/_json_shred.py:672-729 (function _buffer_to_frame) in full. COMPLEXITY IS INCIDENTAL: the two guards are the identical shape `if col_type in <set> and any(isinstance(v,<pytype>) for v in values): raise ApiInputSchemaError(<msg>, column=col_name, declared_type=col_type)`; the only variation is data (type-set, python type, message), so a 2-row table + loop is a legitimate de-duplication, not loss of an essential case. BEHAVIOR-PRESERVING (every case traced): (1) MUTUAL EXCLUSION confirmed — guard 1 fires only for col_type in {int,float}, guard 2 only for col_type=='date'; the sets are disjoint and col_type is a single value, so at most one guard's col_type predicate is true per column and table-iteration order is irrelevant. (2) BOOL-SUBCLASS-OF-INT preserved — guard1 uses isinstance(v,bool) (catches bools in numeric cols); guard2 uses isinstance(v,int), and because bool subset int, isinstance(True,int) is True, so the date guard still rejects bools (test test_bool_in_date_column_rejected_loud relies on this); the table stores `bool` for the numeric guard and `int` for the date guard, preserving both exactly. (3) NULLS — isinstance(None,bool)/isinstance(None,int) are both False, so neither guard fires on None; the strict pl.Series build then handles nulls (test test_iso_strings_and_nulls_build_correct_dates). Unchanged. (4) EMPTY rows — values=[], any(...) over empty is False, no guard fires. Unchanged. (5) FLOAT-in-int / STR-in-date and the try/except re-wrap of (PolarsError,TypeError,OverflowError,ValueError) at lines 719-728 are OUTSIDE this proposal and untouched. EXCEPTION CONTRACT preserved: ApiInputSchemaError(HauteError) takes message + arbitrary kwargs; proposal keeps column=col_name, declared_type=col_type identically. MESSAGE/TEST CHECK: tests assert only substrings — test_build_bool_in_numeric_column_fails_loud asserts 'flag' and 'boolean' (lower); date tests assert match='start' (col name, from col_name not the constant) and 'date' in str; route test asserts type=='ApiInputSchemaError' and 'start' in detail. Grep for the full message strings across tests/ returns NO matches, so no test pins exact prose — moving messages to constants verbatim is safe. ONE IMPLEMENTATION CAUTION (dormant here, not a logic defect): the proposal's `msg.format(col=...,t=...)` requires translating f-string `{col_name!r}` to `{col!r}` (str.format DOES support !r) and keeping the date message's literal `'date'` hardcoded; str.format would also choke on any unescaped literal `{`/`}` in the bodies — but neither current message contains literal braces (examples use parens/quotes), so it is safe. MARGINAL rather than sound because: net module LOC is flat (messages just relocate), the readability gain is locality only, and a 2-entry table + 3 named constants + msg.format indirection is a borderline trade vs two explicit inline guards — a judgment call, not a clear win, which per the project's 'avoid unnecessary indirection / highest-quality' bar does not clearly clear the churn threshold.
verdict.repro_path: N/A (read-only trace; no behavioral repro needed — proposal is provably behavior-preserving). Existing coverage: tests/test_scalar_array_and_inference.py:427 (bool-in-numeric), tests/test_json_cache_integrity.py:998-1056 (date-rejects-int/bool/mixed, iso-ok, route-422).
verdict.recommended_action: OPTIONAL. If applied: introduce module-level `_SILENT_COERCION_GUARDS = ((frozenset({'int','float'}), bool, _MSG_BOOL_IN_NUMERIC), (frozenset({'date'}), int, _MSG_INT_IN_DATE))` with the two messages as named constants COPIED VERBATIM, and a 4-line loop `for types, pytype, msg in _SILENT_COERCION_GUARDS: if col_type in types and any(isinstance(v, pytype) for v in values): raise ApiInputSchemaError(msg.format(col=col_name, t=col_type), column=col_name, declared_type=col_type)`. Implementer MUST: (a) keep `{col!r}` / `{t!r}` conversions matching the original `!r` repr quoting, (b) keep the date message's literal `'date'` hardcoded (col_type may also be passed but need not be referenced), (c) leave the strict pl.Series build + its except block at 719-728 unchanged. Then run tests/test_scalar_array_and_inference.py and tests/test_json_cache_integrity.py::TestDateColumnsRejectJsonNumbers to confirm the 'boolean'/'date'/column-name substrings still surface. Given the modest, locality-only benefit and the 2-row-table tradeoff, leaving the two explicit guards as-is is equally defensible.

item.what_it_does: Recursively converts a value into a JSON-safe, order-independent canonical form and provides a cross-type sort key for set members.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL: _canonicalise and _sort_key are two parallel isinstance ladders over the SAME type universe (None/bool/int|float/str/list|tuple/set|frozenset/Mapping), encoding the type taxonomy twice. The 'tag, value' ordering in _sort_key and the recursive dispatch in _canonicalise must be kept in lockstep by hand; a new supported type means editing two ladders.
item.current_metrics: _canonicalise len ~48 cx ~9; _sort_key len ~26 cx ~8.
item.proposal: Keep the two functions (they have distinct jobs) but drive both from one ordered type table, e.g. `_TYPE_TAGS = (('0_none', type(None)), ('1_bool', bool), ('2_num', (int,float)), ('3_str', str), ('4_list', list), ('5_dict', dict))`, and have _sort_key look up its tag from that table. This makes the taxonomy single-sourced; _canonicalise can assert membership against the same table so an unsupported type fails loud in exactly one place. (Conservative variant: just add a shared `_canonical_type_tag(value)` used by _sort_key, leaving _canonicalise's structure as-is.)
item.behavior_preservation: Tag strings ('0_none'..'5_dict') and their ordering are preserved verbatim, so sorted() output for any set is byte-identical. bool-before-int ordering is preserved by listing bool before (int,float) in the table (isinstance(True,int) is True, so order in the table is load-bearing and must match the current hand-written order). The TypeError-on-unsupported behaviour is retained.
item.est_reduction: ~10-15 LOC and removes a two-ladder maintenance coupling; modest cx reduction.

verdict.evidence:
The proposal's premise — "_canonicalise and _sort_key are two parallel isinstance ladders over the SAME type universe" — is factually false, and the consequences make the table-drive either behavior-breaking or net-zero.

TWO DIFFERENT TYPE UNIVERSES (the core defect):
- _canonicalise (src/haute/_cache.py:113-160) dispatches on INPUT types: None, str/int/float/bool, list+tuple, set+frozenset, AND any collections.abc.Mapping. Its branches collapse tuple->list, set/frozenset->sorted list, every Mapping->plain dict.
- _sort_key (lines 163-188) runs AFTER _canonicalise, on already-canonical JSON-safe values, so it dispatches on OUTPUT types: None, bool, int/float, str, list, dict. It deliberately checks `list`/`dict` and NEVER tuple/set/frozenset/Mapping, because by then those no longer exist. The taxonomy is not duplicated; the two functions are two stages of a pipeline with intentionally different type sets.

The proposed shared table `_TYPE_TAGS = (..., ('4_list', list), ('5_dict', dict))` stops at list/dict. If _canonicalise "asserts membership against the same table" (as proposed), valid inputs set, frozenset, tuple, and non-dict Mappings (MappingProxyType/OrderedDict — pinned by test_caching_correctness.py::test_any_mapping_encodes_like_a_plain_dict) would be REJECTED, changing digests and breaking the cache. Unsound.

_sort_key cannot be table-driven either: its second tuple element is load-bearing and uses FOUR distinct expressions per branch — None->literal 0; bool->raw value; (int,float)->raw value (numeric order, pinned by test_set_members_sort_numerically_not_by_json_text); str->RAW value, i.e. code-point order NOT JSON text (pinned by test_set_strings_sort_by_code_point_not_escape_text); list->_canonical_dumps(value); dict->_canonical_dumps(value) (lists/dicts aren't cross-instance orderable). A table of (tag,type) only single-sources the FIRST element; reproducing the rest needs a parallel table of value-extractor callables — exactly the two-part hand-kept structure the proposal claims to delete, and less readable.

bool-before-int: current code already orders the `isinstance(value, bool)` branch before `(int,float)` in BOTH functions. The table preserves this only via iteration order, relocating a load-bearing constraint into a more fragile data-driven form where its load-bearing nature is LESS obvious than an explicit first `if isinstance(value, bool)`.

Conservative variant (shared `_canonical_type_tag` used only by _sort_key) is behavior-safe but yields ~0 LOC: _sort_key still needs the full per-branch ladder for the value component; it only adds an indirection.

Complexity is ESSENTIAL (deliberate input-normalisation vs canonical-output-ordering contract on differing type universes), not incidental. Claimed ~10-15 LOC reduction is unachievable without breaking behavior or adding a second parallel structure. On digest-critical single-source-of-truth code (module docstrings lines 71-99 warn one-byte drift = silent cache collisions), the risk outweighs the non-existent payoff.
verdict.est_reduction: ~0 LOC realistically. The advertised 10-15 LOC is not achievable: the aggressive table-drive variant changes behavior (rejects valid set/frozenset/non-dict-Mapping inputs in _canonicalise); the conservative _canonical_type_tag variant nets ~0 lines while adding indirection.
verdict.repro_path: Read src/haute/_cache.py:113-188 and contrast the isinstance targets: _canonicalise checks (list,tuple)/(set,frozenset)/Mapping; _sort_key checks list/dict. Then read tests/test_caching_correctness.py:414-561 and tests/test_infrastructure_contracts.py:80-97 for the pinned ordering/value-component contracts.
verdict.recommended_action: Reject. Leave both functions as-is. The premise (same type universe / duplicated taxonomy) is incorrect — _sort_key dispatches on post-canonicalisation types (list/dict) while _canonicalise dispatches on pre-canonicalisation input types (tuple/set/frozenset/Mapping), so no single table can drive both. If any clarity gain is desired, the only safe move is a one-line comment on each function noting the bool-before-int ordering and the input-vs-canonical-universe distinction — not a table-drive. Preserve the existing tests as the behavioral lock.

item.what_it_does: Yields top-level dict records from JSONL (per non-blank line) or JSON (root array element / root object), counting non-object inputs as skips.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL: the 'parse one candidate; if isinstance dict yield else _count_record_skip()' decision is written three times (JSONL loop 349-352, JSON-array loop 359-363, JSON-root-object/else 364-367). The yield-or-count rule is one concept fragmented across the two file-format branches.
item.current_metrics: _iter_records len ~50, cx ~9, nest 3.
item.proposal: Factor a tiny `_emit_record(obj) -> Iterator[dict]` (or inline `def _maybe(obj)`) that does `if isinstance(obj, dict): yield obj; else: _count_record_skip()`, and have all three sites `yield from _maybe(obj)`. item.title: infer_v2_schema_from_data over-widens a pure-int/float scalar-array column to 'str' when an EARLIER record had the same key as an empty array []
item.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:1160-1181 (the empty-array `scalar_tables.setdefault(child, "str")` at 1164-1165 then `scalar_tables[child] = _widen_type(scalar_tables.get(child), elem_type or "str")` at 1181)
item.failure_scenario: Data file: record 1 has `{"tags": []}`, record 2 has `{"tags": [1, 2, 3]}`. On record 1 the empty-array branch runs `scalar_tables.setdefault(('tags',), 'str')` -> 'str'. On record 2 the scalar-array branch computes elem_type='int' but then `scalar_tables[('tags',)] = _widen_type('str', 'int')` = 'str' (int+str disagreement widens to str). The inferred scalar child table types its `value` column as 'str' even though every NON-empty element is an int. The user accepts the inferred schema; the built parquet column is String, and any downstream numeric rating/banding on that column is silently wrong (string '1' not int 1). Order-dependent: if the empty array appears AFTER a populated one, _widen_type('int','int')='int' first, then 'int'+'str'(from empty)... still ends 'str' — so it is consistently wrong whenever any empty array co-occurs with a populated scalar array at the same key. The docstring claims the object branch 'wins at table-assembly time' for empties, but that only covers object-vs-empty, not scalar-vs-empty: a scalar-array key never enters object_cols, so the over-widened 'str' is what assembly emits.

verdict.repro_path: C:\Users\prici\haute\review\03-simplification\repro\cache__BUG-N1.py
verdict.evidence: Executed repro (exit 0) against the real infer_v2_schema_from_data via a tempfile JSONL. Assembly 1199-1209 emits a scalar child table (('tags',) in scalar_tables, not in object_cols) with value col type 'str'. Impact confirmed: _coerce_scalar(1,'str') (line 96-97) -> "1", and _POLARS_TYPE_MAP['str']=pl.String (666) -> the built parquet value column is String holding '1','2','3'; downstream numeric rating/banding is silently wrong with no loud failure. CLAIM CORRECTION (disproven by Case B [{"tags":[1,2,3]},{"tags":[]}] -> 'int', exit-0 assert): the claim's statement that it is "consistently wrong whenever any empty array co-occurs" / wrong even when the empty appears AFTER a populated array is FALSE — the empty branch uses setdefault() (not assignment), so a trailing empty [] is a no-op and a pre-existing 'int' is preserved. item.title: _iter_sampled_json_array_records does NOT count skipped non-object records, so inference sampling silently drops scalars/nested-arrays that the full path would surface via skip accounting
item.location: src/haute/_json_shred.py:425-429 (the sampled reader's `if isinstance(obj, dict): yield obj; yielded += 1` with no else-skip-count) vs _iter_records:358-367 which counts non-object root-array elements
item.failure_scenario: This is an inference-path inconsistency rather than a build-path data loss, but it makes inference SHAPE-BLIND vs the build. For a root array like `[1, {"a":1}, [2,3], {"a":2}]` with sample_size set, the sampled reader parses `1` and `[2,3]`, finds them non-dict, and silently advances without recording that two top-level inputs were non-records; the unsampled/full inference path (`_iter_records`) has no stats either when called from inference (stats defaults None), so the asymmetry is only observable as 'sampled inference may scan past an arbitrary number of junk elements before collecting N objects, with no signal'. More concretely the loop `while yielded < sample_size` can read FAR past sample_size elements (every scalar/array element is consumed but not counted toward the cap), so a malformed-but-parseable prefix of thousands of scalars is fully streamed during a 'sampled' inference, defeating the stated purpose ('stops after the requested object records'). The bytes are still validated for JSON well-formedness, but the cost/early-stop contract in the docstring ('the iterator stops after the requested object records instead of reading the rest of the file') is violated for arrays dominated by non-object elements.

verdict.repro_path: C:\Users\prici\haute\review\03-simplification\repro\cache__BUG-N2.py
verdict.evidence:
Catalog: Grep for "BUG-N2", "_iter_sampled_json_array_records", "stops after the requested", "sample_size", "skipped non-object" in review/02-findings/catalog.md => 0 matches (this is a NEW claim, not a duplicate).

The CODE behavior is real: _json_shred.py:415-429 — `while yielded < sample_size:` increments `yielded` only inside `if isinstance(obj, dict):` (line 427-429), so non-object root-array elements are consumed without counting toward the cap. Repro with `[0..4999, {a:1}, {a:2}, ...]`, sample_size=2 => consumed 5002 top-level elements to yield 2 objects (printed "top-level elements consumed= 5002").

BUT the bug FRAMING is refuted on every prong, proven by two additional executed traces:

1) CONTRACT IS ABOUT OBJECT RECORDS, NOT ELEMENTS. infer_v2_schema_from_data docstring (line 1128-1130) and _iter_sampled_json_array_records docstring (line 378) both denominate the stop condition in "object records", never in array elements. Nothing claims to bound elements read.

2) "Defeats 'stops after the requested object records'" is FALSE. Objects-FIRST test (`[{a:1},{a:2}, 0..4999]`, sample_size=2): reader consumed exactly 2 elements and STOPPED — the 5000-scalar tail was untouched (`tail of 5000 scalars read? False`). Objects-IN-MIDDLE test (`[0..4999, {a:1},{a:2}, 0..4999]`, 10002 elems): sampled consumed 5002 elements and skipped the 5000-element tail, whereas full `_iter_records` read_bytes() the ENTIRE file. So the sampled reader DOES "stop after the requested object records instead of reading the rest of the file" and is strictly cheaper than the full path. The 5002 in the first repro is irreducible: the 2 objects physically follow 5000 scalars, so ANY reader must pass them to reach the 2nd object.

3) "Shape-blind / silently drops scalars/nested-arrays the full path would surface via skip accounting" is FALSE. The claim itself concedes inference passes no stats on EITHER path: _iter_records_for_inference calls `_iter_records(data_path)` with no stats (lines 493, 496) and the sampled reader has no stats param at all — so both inference paths discard skip info, i.e. they are mutually CONSISTENT. ShredSkipStats is consumed only on the BUILD path (line 825, which uses _iter_records and never the sampled reader). Top-level non-object array elements are not records and carry no schema; scalars/nested arrays INSIDE object records are walked identically by _walk (line 1145+). No schema/shape information is lost; the build is unaffected.

Net: the code matches its documented contract exactly; there is no data loss, no contract violation, and no observable inference inconsistency. The "reads many elements" property is the necessary cost of locating N objects and the sampled path remains strictly less work than the full path.
verdict.recommended_action: Reject BUG-N2 — non-bug. The early-stop contract is denominated in "object records" and the reader honors it precisely (executed proof: stops immediately upon collecting sample_size objects, skips remaining tail; strictly cheaper than the full read_bytes path). The skip-counting "asymmetry" is within-inference consistent (neither inference path passes stats) and the only stats consumer is the build path, which never uses the sampled reader. No fix needed. If the team nonetheless wants a hard element cap for adversarial/DoS-shaped inputs (a malicious all-scalar prefix of unbounded length with no objects), that is a NEW hardening feature, not a correctness fix, and should be filed separately; note the input is still fully JSON-validated by orjson.loads per element.
verdict.est_reduction: n/a

item.title: _canonical_dumps passes sort_keys=True to json.dumps after _canonicalise already sorted/canonicalised, but the set-member sort in _sort_key orders strings by Python code point while json.dumps(ensure_ascii=True) escapes non-ASCII — a frozenset of non-ASCII strings inside a list/dict member is sorted by raw code point yet SERIALIZED escaped, which is correct, but two DISTINCT sets that differ only by member order in a nested list are NOT re-sorted by json.dumps
item.location: src/haute/_cache.py:103-110 (_canonical_dumps with sort_keys=True) and :180-185 (_sort_key for list/dict members uses _canonical_dumps of the member)
item.failure_scenario: _canonicalise converts a set to a sorted list (order-independent), but a list/tuple is preserved in element order (correct — lists are ordered). The risk is the nested-set ordering key: _sort_key for a list/dict member returns `_canonical_dumps(value)` which itself applies sort_keys=True. For a set whose members are dicts, the members were already canonicalised (key-sorted) by _canonicalise before _sort_key sees them, so the json.dumps(sort_keys=True) is a redundant second sort that is harmless. HOWEVER for a set whose members are LISTS, _sort_key serializes the list verbatim (json arrays are order-preserving), so two set-members that are the same multiset in different order (e.g. {[1,2],[2,1]}) sort to DIFFERENT keys and both survive — which is the intended set semantics. The actual latent defect: json.dumps with sort_keys=True is applied to a structure that contains canonicalised dicts AND the redundant sort means a future change to _canonicalise (e.g. dropping its own dict key-sort because 'json.dumps sorts anyway') would silently still pass because _canonical_dumps re-sorts — the two layers mask each other. This is a fragility/redundancy that can hide a real canonicalisation regression rather than a live mis-digest today; flagged as low-confidence latent.

verdict.repro_path: C:\Users\prici\haute\review\03-simplification\repro\cache__BUG-N4.py
verdict.evidence: Central premise contradicted by code + repro. P1: _canonicalise (src/haute/_cache.py:148-156) does NOT sort dict keys — it preserves insertion order (repro: input ['b','a','c'] -> _canonicalise output ['b','a','c']). The SOLE key-ordering authority is json.dumps(sort_keys=True) in _canonical_dumps (_cache.py:103-110). Therefore there is exactly ONE key sort, not two — the claim's 'redundant second sort' / 'two layers mask each other' mechanism for dict keys does not exist as described. P2 (claim concedes 'correct'): non-ASCII set members sort by code point via _sort_key (_cache.py:163-188) and serialize ASCII-escaped — byte-exact canonical_json(frozenset({chr(0xE9),'z'})) == '[\"z\",\"\\u00e9\"]' (z<U+00E9 by code point; escaped), order-independent across insertion order. (The lone 'False' in the main repro P2 line is a Windows cp1252 console display artifact on the source 'e-acute' literal; the actual emitted value printed two lines above is correct, and a code-point-only re-check matched exactly.) P3: json.dumps(sort_keys=True) can ONLY reorder dict keys; it cannot mask set->list conversion, set-member sorting, tuple->list, or type rejection — _canonicalise's unique jobs (raw set -> TypeError). Repro EXIT=0; git status shows only review/ touched (no src/tests/rating). The claim is self-labelled 'low-confidence latent' and 'not a live mis-digest today' — verification confirms NO live bug and the masking/redundancy framing is factually wrong.
verdict.est_reduction: none
verdict.recommended_action: Reject BUG-N4 — do not catalog as a bug. No code change warranted: there is no live mis-digest (claim concedes this), and the asserted fragility ('two layers mask each other' for dict-key sorting) is contradicted by the source — _canonicalise does not sort dict keys, so json.dumps(sort_keys=True) is a single non-redundant authority, not a masking second sort. The non-ASCII/escaping behaviour the claim itself calls 'correct' is byte-exact-correct. If anything, sort_keys=True is the deliberate, sole key-orderer and removing it would be the regression. Not a catalog candidate; verified absent from catalog.md (searched BUG-N4, sort_keys, _canonical_dumps, _canonicalise, _sort_key, double/redundant-sort — no match).

verdict.evidence:
The proposal bundles two changes of unequal merit.

(1) DEAD-BRANCH REMOVAL `d.get("iteration", i)` -> `d["iteration"]` (_charts.py:310): SOUND and provably behaviour-preserving. The proposal names two producers; there are actually THREE, all of which unconditionally set "iteration": CPU callback _algorithms.py:194 `history_entry = {"iteration": float(it)}`; GPU reconstruction _algorithms.py:574 and :580 both `loss_history.append({"iteration": i})`; and the omitted GLM producer _rustystats.py:255-256 `[{"iteration": 1.0, "train_deviance": ...}]`. Every test fixture in tests/test_charts.py (lines 222, 241, 250, 581, 588, 596, 603) also includes "iteration". So the `.get` default is never taken by any real or test caller. Stronger: the default value `i` comes from `enumerate(data)` AFTER subsampling re-slices `data = [loss_history[i] for i in sorted_idx]` (line 307), so `i` is the post-subsample positional index, NOT the original iteration number. If the fallback ever fired it would emit wrong x-values for subsampled curves -- it is incoherent dead code, not a meaningful guard. Replacing with `d["iteration"]` changes behaviour for zero real inputs.

(2) EXTRACT `_subsample_indices(n, target, *, must_keep)`: behaviour-preserving but MARGINAL. The mechanical extraction reproduces the selection exactly: `step = n/300`; `{int(i*step) for i in range(300)}` (floor-rounded, i=0 -> 0) `| {0, n-1}` `| {best_iteration if 0 <= best_iteration < n}`, then `sorted(...)` ascending. Conditional inclusion of best_iteration must stay at the call site or be filtered in the helper -- either is identical. HOWEVER the justification "reused conceptually by other point-limited charts" is factually FALSE: grep over _charts.py shows the subsample pattern (`len(data) > 300`, `int(i*step)`) appears at exactly ONE site (line 297-307); no other chart point-limits, and no `_subsample_indices` exists anywhere. Extracting a single-use ~6-LOC block into a separate function is a lateral move (indirection for inline locality), not a clear simplification, and adds churn plus a new test surface for no current consumer (YAGNI). The complexity here is INCIDENTAL (removable) but the structural refactor is not clearly worthwhile, which drags the bundled proposal to marginal.

Net: take part (1) -- the genuine, low-risk dead-code win; defer part (2) until a second point-limited chart actually needs the helper. The proposal's "maximal caution" fallback inverts the value (it would keep the dead .get and only extract the helper -- exactly backwards).

verdict.recommended_action: Accept ONLY the one-line change: `iterations = [d["iteration"] for d in data]` (drop the `, i` enumerate fallback at _charts.py:310). item.what_it_does: Collects GLM fit statistics, reading some as attributes and some as zero-arg methods, each guarded by try/except that logs a warning on failure.
item.why_complex: INCIDENTAL (minor). Two near-identical `for (attr/method, label) in [...]: try: stats[label] = float(getattr(model, x)[()]) except Exception as exc: logger.warning('fit_stat_failed', attr=x, error=str(exc))` loops differ only in whether the resolved attribute is called. item.proposal: Unify into one table where each row carries a callable extractor: `_FIT_STATS = [("deviance", lambda m: float(m.deviance)), ("aic", lambda m: float(m.aic())), ("converged", lambda m: 1.0 if m.converged else 0.0), ...]`, then a single `for label, extract in _FIT_STATS: try: stats[label]=extract(model) except Exception as exc: logger.warning('fit_stat_failed', attr=label, error=str(exc))`.
